name: Spare iPhone as a fixed camera
description: A spare iPhone on a stand answers 'what does the porch look like right now' with one still photo on request. Extends F079, which was parked because the house has no network camera.
example: Tony texts: "Is there a package on the porch?"
how: Spare iPhone on a stand and charger with the OpenClaw app open: Allow Camera on, keep-awake on, Guided Access holding the app in the foreground with touch ignored. Add camera.snap to gateway.nodes.commands.allow and approve the widened surface; keep camera.clip in commands.deny. The asking parent's agent (or a small stateless 'look' agent it hands off to) takes one still through an in-house plugin tool that calls api.runtime.nodes.invoke with this node id and camera.snap fixed in code and facing set to back (the default is the front camera). The built-in nodes tool's camera_snap action does the same, but that tool is owner-only, so it would work in Tony's turns only. The photo goes to the vision model and the answer comes back as text. Alternative without the iOS app: Apple's Continuity Camera turns an iPhone (XR or later, on happy's Apple Account) into a camera of the Mac while the phone stays locked, which avoids keeping an app on screen; capturing it needs the OpenClaw Mac app in node mode or the camsnap skill's local-webcam mode, and neither is installed.
depends_on: IPH-01
hardware: spare iPhone, stand, charger, a window or shelf with the right view
decision 3 of the 9 Oct catalog: photos to the cloud vision model under store:false
decision: where a camera is acceptable in the house
decision from IPH-01: a shared spare phone holding an operator token
local vision model before any indoor view
in-house plugin tool over api.runtime.nodes.invoke (the built-in nodes tool is owner-only and sandbox-denied by default)
caveats: iOS prohibits camera use in the background, so the app must stay on screen around the clock. After a crash, an iOS update or a reboot the phone sits at its lock screen and the camera silently stops answering.
One still per request, or a clip of at most 60 seconds. No motion detection, no stream, no history.

A screen that never sleeps on a phone that never leaves the charger wears the battery. The 80 percent charge limit exists only on iPhone 15 and later; an older spare phone has only Optimized Battery Charging.
A cheap network camera with the camsnap skill (F079), or a doorbell's own app, does this job better. The spare phone only wins on price.
Pictures of the home, and of the kids if they walk past, go to the cloud vision model.

camera.snap is switched on for the whole gateway, not for one phone, and Allow Camera defaults to on in the app. A parent's own paired phone becomes a possible camera target unless Allow Camera is switched off there and the hook pins the node.
A phone visible in a window holds a gateway credential (at least read access to every agent's sessions). If it is taken, revoke the device on the gateway straight away.
The roadmap keeps kids' content away from cloud models. With no local vision model, the only defensible view is the porch or driveway, where the kids are incidental.
safety: The agent that looks at the picture reads untrusted content (a note held up to the lens is a prompt injection), so it must hold no memory, mail or message tool; it returns text to the caller. The parent's own agent therefore never calls the camera itself. Porch or driveway views only, never a room the kids use, bedrooms or bathrooms, until a local vision model exists. Clips stay denied so no audio is recorded. Pictures are not written to memory or the wiki. The hook pins the look agent to one node id and the camera_snap action.
unverified: Whether the app's keep-awake setting alone keeps a phone awake and connected for weeks.
Whether a Continuity Camera iPhone shows up in the Mac node's camera list (the camera page only says such formats are left unchanged).
Whether a Continuity Camera iPhone appears in camsnap's local device list.

name: iPhone Shortcuts automations as triggers for Happy
description: Events on a parent's iPhone (arriving, CarPlay, plugging in, an NFC tag, a Focus) can nudge Happy without anyone typing, using Apple's own automation engine. The reverse direction, Happy making a phone run a shortcut, is possible only by sending the phone a keyword message.
example: Trigger: Jordan's phone connects to CarPlay on a weekday afternoon, and Happy texts her today's pickup notes.
how:
Phone to Happy: a personal automation in Shortcuts on the parent's phone, set to run without asking, whose action is Get Contents of URL with a POST to a gateway hook over the tailnet. The request must carry the hook token in an Authorization or x-openclaw-token header; proving that the shortcut can send that header is the first test. On the gateway: hooks.enabled, a dedicated hooks.token, hooks.allowedAgentIds limited to one agent for that parent (the roadmap's

-jobs agent once it exists), and a hooks.mappings entry that turns an event id into a fixed wake or agent action. Happy to phone: a Message-trigger automation on the phone (sender is Happy, message contains a keyword) that runs a shortcut such as 'open the OpenClaw app' or 'set a Focus'; Happy sends the keyword through an in-house tool that only knows a fixed keyword list. The Mac's own shortcuts command stays under F078.
depends_on: Tailscale on the phone
gateway hooks (off by default) with a mapping per event and a dedicated tool-less events agent, or a host-side relay in front of the hook
for the reverse direction: the phone's handle on the pinned recipient list and an in-house keyword tool

a target agent for the hook: the roadmap's

-jobs agents are planned for a later milestone and do not exist yet
first test: a shortcut that sends the token header to the hook
caveats: Automations belong to one device and sync to other devices switched off, so each parent builds their own.

Apple lists the triggers that may run without asking (time of day, arrive, leave, CarPlay, email, message, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, charger, sound recognition and others). A Notification trigger exists but is not on that list, so it cannot be an unattended notification relay.
The hook token sits inside a shortcut on the phone, readable by anyone holding the unlocked phone.
Find My and Focus schedules already cover arrive and leave alerts. Use this where Happy adds something.
The only Shortcuts action the OpenClaw app documents is Start Live Voice, so 'tell Happy' has to go through a web request or a message.

The reverse direction is experimental. I found no Apple-documented way for a Mac to run a shortcut on another device; the keyword message is a workaround, and a phone that shares happy's Apple Account may not treat Happy's own message as incoming.

hooks.token is one shared secret for the whole hook surface. Whoever holds it can also post free text to the wake and agent endpoints for any agent in allowedAgentIds, wake text arrives as a trusted system event, and custom mappings cannot switch those two endpoints off. The allowed agent must therefore be one where injected text can do no harm.
One token means both parents' phones hold the same secret; the hook cannot tell Tony's phone from Jordan's.

Reverse direction: the Message trigger fires on any message from Happy that contains the keyword, including an ordinary reply the model was talked into writing. Use a random keyword, strip it from normal replies in a message hook, and keep the shortcut harmless.

A schedule on the gateway already covers 'pickup notes on weekday afternoons' with no phone-side setup. Phone triggers are worth it only where the phone knows something the gateway does not (in the car, at a place).

Apple lists the automations that can run automatically (time of day, alarm, sleep, arrive, leave, CarPlay, email, message, transaction, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, app, charger, battery level, sound recognition and others). A Notification trigger exists but is not on that list. Apple does not say outright that it always asks, so test it before ruling a notification relay in or out.
safety:
A wake is treated as a trusted system event, so nothing free-text from a phone may reach a private agent. The hook's allowed agent is a tool-less, memory-less events agent, never

-main (memory) or

-jobs (résumé plus browser); the mapping emits fixed strings chosen by event id; delivery is done by code to the owner. Hooks stay tailnet-only with their own token. For the reverse direction the keyword list is fixed in code, the sender filter is pinned, and the shortcut does only harmless things: no unlocking, no purchases, no Home scenes that touch locks or the garage.
unverified: That Get Contents of URL can send the Authorization header the hook requires. Tokens in the query string are rejected, and the Apple page I fetched documents methods and request body but not headers.
Which shortcut actions (opening an app, sending a message) really run while the phone is locked.
Whether a Message trigger fires for a message sent from the same Apple Account.
The list of Shortcuts actions for Messages, location, Focus and Home: the Apple pages I fetched cover triggers and the web-request action only.
Whether Tailscale on the phone is connected at the moment a background automation fires.
Whether a Shortcuts action that sends a message to Happy can run unattended. If it can, the phone could trigger Happy over the existing iMessage channel, as its owner, with no gateway hook at all.

review_notes: The Apple side checks out, but the hook token is one shared secret that also opens the free-text wake and agent endpoints for every allowed agent. Keeping it in a phone shortcut and pointing it at a parent's jobs agent (résumé plus browser) is the wrong placement, and the reverse-direction keyword fires on any Happy message that contains it.

The gateway hook facts and the Apple trigger facts are all confirmed. Three corrections: Apple's page omits the Notification trigger from the run-automatically list but does not say it cannot, the header the hook needs is still not documented by Apple, and the per-person jobs agent the hook should target does not exist yet.

name: An idle Android phone that Happy can actually operate
description: If the goal is an idle phone Happy can operate, OpenClaw documents that for Android, not iPhone: the Android app can expose the screen as a structured element list and perform taps, text entry and swipes.
example: Tony texts: "Check the team app for tomorrow's game time." (A request from Jordan would not reach mobile_ui, which is owner-only.)
how: A cheap Android phone on a charger with the OpenClaw Android app, whose foreground service keeps the gateway connection alive. Turning on Accessibility Control in the app makes the node advertise mobile.ui.observe and mobile.ui.act (in the Android default allowlist; enabled on the phone, then approved as a pairing update). The built-in mobile_ui tool reads a semantic snapshot (text, roles, bounds) and performs one action per call; state-changing actions come back as confirmation_required until the model repeats the call with confirmed set. Give the tool to one stateless phone agent with tools.alsoAllow plus tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow (mobile_ui is on the sandbox default deny list), and expect it to work only in turns started by the command owner, because it is an owner-only core tool. scrcpy lets Tony watch or drive the same phone from the Mac.
depends_on: hardware: an Android phone and a Google account for it
the school or team app must exist on Android
a dedicated stateless phone agent
parent approval hook for state-changing actions (IPH-07)
the request must come from the command owner (or Jordan is added to commands.ownerAllowFrom, which also gives her every owner-only command)
caveats: A second ecosystem to patch and babysit in an all-Apple house.
The docs pages mention mobile UI control only in the command-policy table. The tool is present in the installed code but has no guide page, so treat it as early.
The confirmed flag is the model confirming to itself; a real parent approval has to be added by hook.
It reads element text instead of pixels, so it is faster and steadier than iPhone Mirroring, but apps that draw custom views or mark content as secure will not be readable.

gateway.nodes.commands.deny is global. Denying callLog.search or notifications.list for this phone removes them for every node, and denying a shared command such as contacts.search would also switch it off for a parent's iPhone. Narrow this phone by what it is granted and which surface is approved, not only by the deny list.

A before_tool_call hook sees the action type and an element reference or coordinates, not the app or the label being tapped (the tool keeps the screen snapshot to itself). A parent approval prompt needs extra plumbing to say what is about to be pressed.
The built-in confirmation step looks for English keywords such as pay, send, delete and install. It is a hint to the model, not a control.
Like the iPhone app, the Android app pairs with an operator session as well as a node (see IPH-01).
For this family the school apps already notify both parents' iPhones; weekly use is unlikely to justify a second phone ecosystem.

A paired Android node can post notification events, voice transcripts and agent requests to a session key the phone chooses, so the phone itself is a way into any session. Keep it physically secured and leave notification forwarding off unless IPH-15 is built.
safety: Same trifecta exposure as IPH-08. On the phone: only the target apps, no payment method, no wallet. On the gateway: keep sms.send and sms.search out of commands.allow and add them and callLog.search to commands.deny; mobile_ui only on the stateless agent; a before_tool_call hook requires a parent approval for any act other than scroll, wait or observe. The phone agent holds only mobile_ui: no nodes tool, no memory, no web, no message tool.
unverified: Whether the Google Play build offers Accessibility Control and SMS or only the sideloaded APK does. Google restricts SMS permissions to default handler apps, and the docs say Play builds lack background location.
How Android battery optimisation treats the foreground service over weeks.
Whether any released Android build actually ships the Accessibility Control switch: the Android app page in the installed docs does not mention it; only the gateway-side tool and the policy table do.
Whether a scheduled run counts as an owner turn for mobile_ui.

name: Relay notifications from chosen apps (Android only)
description: The realistic version of 'tell me when the school app pings': an Android phone forwards notifications from an allowlist of apps to the gateway, and a tool-less reader turns each into one line for the parents. The OpenClaw iPhone app has no equivalent.
example: Trigger: the team app notifies "Practice moved to 5:30" and both parents get that line by iMessage.
how: On the Android phone: Forward Notification Events on (off by default, needs Notification Listener access), Package Filter set to Allowlist with only the school and sports app ids, the per-minute cap left at 20, and Route Session Key pointing at a dedicated session. On the gateway: each forwarded notification is queued as a system event on the session key the phone sends, or on the system main session if none is set, with title and text cut to 120 characters each, and that session is woken. Point the key at a session of a reader agent with no tools and no memory. The reader's reply has no channel of its own, so an in-house plugin has to pick up its short structured output and send it to the pinned parents (the family delivery primitive, G009).
depends_on: hardware: an Android phone logged in to the apps (shared with IPH-14)
reader-agent pattern from the mail plan (G015)
family delivery primitive (G009) and notification policy (G001)
caveats: A notification carries a title and a short preview, and the gateway keeps at most 120 characters of each. No full post, no attachments.
Never use the default Blocklist mode: it forwards everything except the listed apps, including one-time codes and bank alerts.
On iPhone this cannot run unattended: the OpenClaw iOS node has no notification commands, and Apple's Notification trigger in Shortcuts is not among the triggers allowed to run without asking.
If the app offers email notifications, the school mailbox path (F051) is simpler and needs no extra phone.

In the installed gateway a forwarded notification is queued as a system event, the same trusted lane as a hook wake, not as safety-wrapped external content. The title and text come from whoever posted in the app.

The session it lands in is named by the phone. With no Route Session Key it falls back to the system main session, which the roadmap keeps on tony-main. One wrong setting on the phone puts strangers' text into a private agent as system text.
Both parents already get these notifications on their own iPhones. The relay earns its place only if Happy does something more with them, such as a digest or spotting a schedule change.
Needs an Android phone and a Google account the family does not own.

The OpenClaw iPhone app has no notification commands. Shortcuts on iPhone has a Notification trigger, but Apple does not list it among automations that can run automatically, so an unattended relay from an iPhone is unconfirmed.
If Route Session Key is left empty the events land in the system main session. Set it before turning forwarding on.
safety: Notification text is untrusted content that arrives on a trusted lane, so the only acceptable target is a reader with no tools and no memory, exactly like the mail readers, with delivery done by code to pinned recipients. Route Session Key must be set, and checked again after every app update, because the default route is a private agent's main session. The package allowlist is the hard limit that keeps 2FA codes and financial alerts out. The phone holds no personal accounts beyond the school and team logins.
unverified: How the gateway turns a forwarded notification event into an agent turn (the docs describe the phone's settings, not the gateway side).
How much text each app puts in its notifications.
How the reader's output gets from that session to the delivery code (I found no documented hook for this path).
Whether anything on the gateway can reject notification events aimed at a session other than the reader's.
How to capture a tool-less reader's reply to a system-event wake and hand it to delivery code; I found no documented pattern for it.

name: Accessibility routes: Switch Control and Voice Control
description: Apple's accessibility features can operate an iPhone without touching it, but they are built for a person with a switch or a voice, not for a program. Neither gives Happy a usable control channel.
example: A parent asks: "Can't Happy just use Voice Control on the old phone?"
how: Switch Control: a Mac running Switch Control can take over another Apple device on the same Wi-Fi network and Apple Account, but a person operates it by stepping through an on-screen scanner. The only way for Happy to use it would be the computer tool clicking the Mac's Switch Control panel, which is slower and weaker than iPhone Mirroring. Voice Control: the phone obeys spoken commands, so Happy would have to play synthesized speech at it from a speaker.
depends_on: no programmatic interface exists to build on
caveats: Neither Apple page describes a scripting or automation interface for these features.
Voice Control does not check who is speaking: the TV, a guest or a child can issue the same commands, and so can any audio Happy plays by mistake.
Both are only useful with the phone awake and, in practice, unlocked.
safety: A phone that obeys any voice in the room while sitting unlocked on a charger fails the rule that limits must be ones the model cannot talk past: here anyone could talk past them. Reject.
unverified: Whether Switch Control from a Mac can operate a locked iPhone (the page does not say).
Whether Voice Control accepts commands on the Lock Screen.

name: Screen Time and app requests by chat
description: 'Happy, give the 8-year-old 30 more minutes' or 'approve that app.' This cannot be done and should not be: Apple delivers these requests to a parent's own Messages with approve buttons, and only an adult marked as parent or guardian in Family Sharing can answer.
example: Jordan texts: 'approve the iPad time request.' Happy replies that only her phone can, and where the request is.
how: No mechanism on this stack. The iMessage channel runs in Basic mode, where private-API actions are unavailable, and the approval lives in Apple's own interface on a parent's or guardian's device. Happy's Apple Account must never be given the parent or guardian role in the family group. What Happy can do instead: a weekly 'review Screen Time' reminder (F007), keep the agreed limits as a fact in the vault (F043), and draft the family media rules.
caveats: The only technical route would be to make Happy's account a parent or guardian and drive the Messages window with screen automation. That would also let a bot approve purchases and downloads.
Approving takes one tap on the parent's phone; there is nothing to save.
Google's equivalent controls live in the Family Link app on the parent's device.
safety: Approving a child's purchases and downloads is a purchase action and sits on the never-list. Parental-control authority stays with the two adults.

description: The answer to 'can Happy manage the kids' devices?' for the non-Apple ones. name: Browser action firewall hook (profile pin, site allowlist, approval before typing, no submit)
description: One in-house plugin that decides in code what each agent's browser may do: which profile, which sites and which actions, all as allowlists that fail closed. Without it the browser tool is all-or-nothing. In this batch it only denies; asking a parent before typing is a later addition for the M6 jobs agent.
example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to switch to another browser profile or to type into a form; the call is refused in code before the browser sees it, and the nightly eval has a case for each.
how: Plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`; the docs also offer a stricter tier, `api.registerTrustedToolPolicy`, which runs before ordinary hooks. It reads `ctx.agentId`, `ctx.requester` and `event.params`. A call can hide its target in three places and the hook must read all of them: the URL is taken from `targetUrl` first and `url` second; an act can arrive as a top-level `kind` or inside a nested `request` object; and act kind `batch` carries a nested `actions` array. Rules per agent, all failing closed: reject any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned, and treat a missing `profile` as a block or fill in the assigned one, because an omitted profile means the default profile; reject `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`; allow `open`/`navigate` only when every URL field present is on an exact hostname list; allow only a listed subset of the tool's 24 actions; treat act kinds as an allowlist as well: block `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize` and `type` with `submit`, block any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ, and return `requireApproval` with `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` for `fill`, `type`, `select`, `click` and the `upload` action. Block gated actions outright when `ctx.requester` is absent (scheduled and system runs). Unknown agent, missing field, unknown kind or parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or runs past 15 seconds. Prompts are answered in the same chat that raised them with a typed `/approve <id> <decision>`; the family's config already has `approvals.plugin` enabled in `session` mode. Lobster is not the gate here: it is disabled in sandboxed contexts.
depends_on: G009 hook pattern (fail-closed before_tool_call)
approval prompts routed to the asking chat
caveats: The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. The safe rule is an approval on every click inside a form, which becomes tedious after three prompts.
Approval waits are capped at ten minutes and an unanswered request denies.
Scheduled runs have no approval route, so approval-gated actions never happen unattended. That is the intended behaviour.

On iMessage the approver list is the channel allowlist, not the requester: the roadmap already notes that approvals are not tied to the person whose agent asked, so prompts must go only to the asking chat.
A navigation allowlist in a hook checks the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next.

Every list has to be default-deny. The installed schema has more ways to act than click, type, fill, select and press: `batch` (a list of nested actions), `clickCoords`, `drag` and `hover`; an act can also arrive inside a nested `request` object; `open` takes `targetUrl` where other actions take `url`; `node` and `dashboard` choose a browser without naming a profile. A hook that checks only `kind`, `url` and `profile`, as first written, can be walked around.
The tool's schema can change with any OpenClaw update. Default-deny keeps a new action blocked until someone allows it, but the hook's eval cases still have to be rerun in each weekly patch window.

An approval prompt that shows the site and a field count does not tell the approver what is being sent; one that shows the values puts a child's details on the approval surface, which the docs advise against. Approval is a brake on mistakes, not a defence against exfiltration.
On iMessage the documented text fallback treats a Like tapback as allow-once. A reflex tapback on the prompt is an approval.
The approval branch has one consumer in the roadmap, the M6 jobs agent. Build and test it there, not in this batch.

Do not rely on scheduled runs having no approval route: the docs say an automation's approval card is delivered to whatever approval surface is connected and the run waits. Keep unattended runs away from gated actions in the hook itself, by blocking when no requester is attached to the call.
With `open` and `navigate` allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the `download` action ever being called.
The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 tool schema and can change on upgrade; the hook needs a contract test that runs after every OpenClaw update.
safety: This is what turns 'the model was told not to' into a limit the model cannot argue past: profile, site and action limits live in code and fail closed, in line with both vendors' guidance to restrict sites and confirm consequential actions. It does not by itself make a logged-in browser safe (see WEB-04). It is in-house code sitting on the security boundary: one parsing mistake is a bypass, so it needs its own injection eval cases before any profile on the host holds a login.
unverified: Whether an approval raised by a spawned sub-agent is delivered to the parent chat that started the task; needs a test.
Whether tapback approval works in iMessage Basic mode; the typed /approve command is the documented fallback.
The parameter names were read from the browser tool's schema source, not observed in a live hook event.

name: Voice guardrails pack (scoped devices, Talk owner, spoken confirmation)
description: One reviewed set of limits that goes in before any voice surface is switched on: voice-only devices get a read-plus-talk credential, Talk has an explicit default owner, realtime voice must confirm aloud before acting, cloud speech providers are switched off in config rather than by instruction, and a house rule says shared-room microphones never reach a memory-holding or cloud-backed agent while kids are around. It narrows what a voice device can do; it does not stop a paired device from reading both adults' agents.
example: Trigger: Tony pairs a new voice device. The happy-inspect check lists paired devices and fails if any voice device holds admin or write scope.
how: Pair by device type with `openclaw qr`. A parent's phone that also chats gets `--limited` (no operator.admin; still operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets). A talk-only client such as a room device gets `--voice-node` (node token plus only operator.read and operator.talk, so no chat.send and no tts.speak). Set `talk.agentId` explicitly, because a multi-agent gateway has no unambiguous Talk owner. Use `talk.realtime.brain: agent-consult` and keep the built-in spoken-confirmation gate. Leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off (its default) so a reply directive cannot move speech to a cloud provider. Add a read-only device and scope listing to the operator's inspect script. For hard per-person enforcement the documented route is `gateway.roles` (named operator roles that restrict agents and scopes for verified identities).
depends_on: decision: may family voice devices hold operator.read
G006 audit digest
G005 kill switch covering Talk sessions
caveats: operator.read is documented as not being a per-person privacy boundary: a talk-only device can still read gateway status and session data across agents.
Talk clients choose the agent (the Watch literally asks which agent), so 'Jordan's device only reaches jordan-main' is not enforced without gateway roles.

There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack. Whoever is near the microphone is the user, and the spoken yes can come from anyone in the room; the FaceTime doc says the same about its own calls.

With roles configured, plain device or bootstrap tokens are rejected for operator connections, so roles change how every app signs in and need a verified identity per person. The docs add that the write scope stays gateway-wide even under roles.

operator.read is broad and is in every pairing profile: session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace. There is no voice credential today that cannot read both adults' agent memory.
A read-plus-talk device probably cannot run the native speech loop, because the chat turn is write-scoped. Least privilege therefore pushes voice devices onto the realtime path, which is cloud audio.
Standalone Watch setup needs the iPhone connected with operator.admin, which conflicts with pairing phones below admin.

Scopes limit which gateway methods a device may call, not which agent it reaches. A device names the session key for its own Talk sessions, and the installed gateway also accepts a node-level voice-transcript event that starts an agent run on whatever session key the device supplies (the main session if none). Pinning a device to one agent needs `gateway.roles` or stays a client-side convention.

Tightening a phone's scope has a price: without operator.admin the app's Settings pages (including this device's Talk and Voice Wake switches) do not open, and standalone Watch voice cannot be set up from that phone.

`talk.agentId` is one value for the whole gateway, so it cannot mean each parent's own agent. Whichever agent it names receives every Talk session that arrives without an agent-prefixed key, so it should be a memory-less one.
The default and the limited handoff both include operator.talk.secrets (read Talk configuration with secrets included).
safety: This entry is the control layer for the voice lens: credential scopes, tool policy, provider switches in config and a host-enforced confirmation are limits the model cannot talk its way past. What it cannot deliver is the section 1b separation between the two adults on app or voice devices, or the kids rule; those need verified role enforcement and a local model, neither of which exists yet. Until then the only compliant voice device is the operator's own.
unverified: Whether the iOS and Watch apps still connect once `gateway.roles` is configured.
Whether a voice-node device can be pinned to exactly one agent.

Whether a voice-node credential can run the native speech loop at all.
Whether the provider fallback chain reaches the Microsoft online voice when a local engine fails (the docs and source say it counts as configured by default).
Whether anything short of `gateway.roles` pins a device to one agent; the installed node-event code takes the session key from the device.
Which agent receives a node voice transcript that carries no session key on this multi-agent config (the installed code falls back to the gateway's main session key).

name: Talk mode on a parent's iPhone (native speech loop)
description: A parent installs the OpenClaw iPhone app and holds a spoken back-and-forth with their own agent: the phone transcribes, the gateway answers as it would a text, and the reply is spoken. The app also adds a Listen action on any reply and a Siri phrase or Action Button shortcut that starts voice. Realistic first step is Tony's phone only: the app is a full gateway client and a device node, and with what is verified today a second adult's phone cannot be held to her own agent.
example: Parent presses the Action Button and says: what is on tomorrow, and do I need to pack anything for soccer?
how: App Store OpenClaw app on each adult iPhone, reaching the gateway over the tailnet (the app connects over LAN or tailnet; this gateway is Tailscale Serve only). Tony generates the pairing code with `openclaw qr --limited` instead of the default admin handoff. `--voice-node` is not for a parent's phone: it drops the write scope, so typed chat (`chat.send`) and the Listen action (`tts.speak`) stop working, and whether Talk still runs is untested. Native Talk is a loop: Apple Speech recognition on the phone, Gateway chat on the chosen agent (tony-main or jordan-main), then `talk.speak` playback. `talk.speak` reads the Talk block, not the `tts` block: set `talk.provider` plus `talk.providers.<id>` to a speech provider (the local engine from VOX-04 can be named there); with no Talk provider the gateway call fails and the docs mention an iPhone system-voice fallback. Keys: `talk.agentId` (owner when the client sends no agent-prefixed session key), `talk.speechLocale`, `talk.silenceTimeoutMs`, `talk.interruptOnSpeech`. Entry points: the inline Talk control, the `Start Live Voice` App Shortcut, the Siri phrase, or the Action Button.
depends_on: OpenClaw iOS app on each adult iPhone
Tailscale on both phones
VOX-03 voice guardrails (pairing profile decision)
a TTS engine: VOX-04 or F004
Tailscale on the phone
decision: is a write-scoped gateway credential on a phone acceptable
a Talk speech provider (talk.provider), configured separately from the tts block
spike before any second adult is paired: gateway.roles with the iOS app
a Talk speech provider under `talk.provider` (the VOX-04 local engine), or accept the iPhone system-voice fallback
caveats: Audio can leave the house even in the native loop: the docs say Apple Speech recognition on iOS may use network services. The transcript then goes to OpenAI as text like any typed message.
iOS may suspend background audio, so voice is best-effort unless the app is in the foreground; the Siri shortcut does not bypass unlock or foreground restrictions.

The default pairing code hands the phone an operator token that includes admin scope, and the app lets its user pick any agent. Per-person separation on this surface is by convention unless VOX-03 is done first. Even the limited code keeps operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets, so the phone can still chat with any agent.

`openclaw qr` only advertises a Tailscale URL when OpenClaw itself owns the Serve route (`gateway.tailscale.mode`), so the M0 Serve setup has to be checked before pairing. The config repo's flat config sets `gateway.tailscale.mode` to serve on a loopback bind, so this looks met; confirm on the live gateway. mDNS discovery is off there, so pairing is by QR or setup code, not by Bonjour.
Dictating an iMessage to Happy with the keyboard microphone or Siri already works today with no setup. Talk adds the continuous loop, barge-in and spoken replies, not a new capability.

The app is a gateway client first. Every pairing profile includes operator.read, which covers session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace; the app's Agents > Files screen and its offline transcript cache show exactly that. On a second adult's phone this means the other adult's agent memory is readable.
The default pairing code includes the admin scope, and in every profile the app lets its user pick any agent.

`--limited` removes only operator.admin. The phone keeps operator.write (chat with any agent, gateway-wide tool invocation, node command relay) and operator.approvals, so a second phone is also a second approver for every pending request.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Pairing registers the phone as the gateway's first node. Once a node surface is approved, the default iOS policy allows location, contacts search, calendar events, reminders and latest photos to any write-scoped client, subject to the iOS permission on the phone.
App Store builds register with a vendor-hosted push relay: a new third-party dependency and egress destination for this gateway.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.
A lost or unlocked phone is now a gateway credential rather than just an iMessage sender; Tony needs the device-revocation step written down before pairing.

A phone paired without operator.admin cannot open the app's Settings pages, which is where this device's Talk, Voice Wake, background-listening and speakerphone switches live. Plan on the inline Talk control in Chat and the Start Live Voice shortcut.
safety:
Tony's phone: acceptable, because section 1b already makes Tony the control-plane owner who can read everything; pair with the limited profile, keep the node surface unapproved, and treat the phone as an admin-adjacent credential. A second adult's phone: no safe placement is verified. The docs describe operator scopes as a guardrail inside one trusted operator domain, not a boundary between people, and the named-roles feature that could limit her to her own agent rejects the device and bootstrap tokens that QR pairing issues. Voice input is the speaker's own words, so no untrusted-content leg is added to

-main, and tool policy, hooks and the family-only recipient pin still apply to the agent's tool calls. A child must not use a parent's Talk session: every agent is cloud-backed and Apple Speech on iOS may send audio to Apple.

adds: The Start Live Voice shortcut for Siri or the Action Button; the vendor-free speech path on an iPhone is the app's on-device fallback, which is unverified for Talk.
Market context (Alexa+ and ChatGPT voice) and the same conclusion: it fits Tony's phone only, because every voice pairing carries read access to all sessions.
review_notes: The iPhone app is a full gateway client and device node, not a voice-only surface: every pairing profile carries operator.read, and the two phone profiles also carry write and approvals, so a second adult's phone can read the other adult's agent workspace and approve anyone's requests. That breaks the section 1b rule that family members only chat; the only safe placement verified today is the operator's own phone.

All 11 sources hold. Two feasibility corrections: a parent's phone needs the `--limited` code, not `--voice-node`, because typed chat and Listen are write-scoped; and Talk playback has its own `talk.provider` block, so the `tts` block from VOX-04 alone does not give `talk.speak` a voice.
